title: Union Nurses Say AI Scheduling Tool Makes Jobs Harder
summary: New research shows HCA's Timpani AI scheduling software and remote monitoring tools are straining nurses, raising accountability questions in healthcare AI
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- HCA's Timpani AI scheduling software, now in 130+ hospitals, reportedly overworks nurses with consecutive shifts and ignores time-off requests.
- AI Now Institute report based on 16 union nurses finds hospitals deploy AI tools rapidly without transparency or accountability frameworks.
- Remote patient monitoring systems raise safety concerns after four UK deaths linked to facilities using Oxevision camera-based technology.


Union nurses working with AI scheduling systems report being assigned six consecutive shifts, having time-off requests ignored, and experiencing dangerous understaffing in intensive care units, according to new research published this week. The AI Now Institute's report, "AI Comes for Nursing," examines how rapidly deployed hospital AI tools are reshaping nursing work, often without transparency or clear accountability when systems fail.


## Timpani Scheduling AI Draws Criticism


HCA Healthcare's Timpani scheduling software, now operational in more than 130 hospitals, sits at the center of the controversy. Built in partnership with Palantir Technologies, the system aims to predict staffing needs 30 days ahead based on patient volumes and staff preferences. Officially launched on November 18, 2026, the AI Now Institute report documents how the tool functions in practice through interviews with frontline nurses.


Luke, a psychiatric nurse in Missouri identified by pseudonym, told researchers no one at his facility can modify the schedules Timpani generates. Control lies with a Nashville-based team reachable only through the app itself. While HCA maintains that nurse leaders can override schedules as patient needs change, interviewed nurses described a system that exacerbates burnout rather than alleviating it. Many feared the algorithm serves primarily as a cost-cutting tool to reduce labor expenses and promote leaner staffing models.


## Research Methodology and Scope


The report draws from eight focus groups with 16 registered nurses across six states, conducted between April and June 2026, plus a September workshop with approximately 60 nurses. All participants belong to National Nurses United, a union representing more than 225,000 healthcare workers. Katie Wells, AI Now senior fellow and co-author, acknowledges the study cannot determine how widespread these experiences are or whether patterns differ across for-profit, nonprofit, and public hospital systems.


HCA responded that feedback from "16 union-affiliated individuals" does not constitute a reasonable measurement of the tool's impact. The company stated that its 100,000 nurses receive 98% of their shift preferences across millions of annual shifts, with schedule changes and swaps available through the Timpani app.


## Remote Monitoring Raises Safety Questions


Patient monitoring AI presents different concerns. Alex, a Nevada nurse, described his hospital replacing dedicated bedside sitters for fall-risk patients with a remote monitoring system where a single worker in Oregon watches multiple patients across five facilities. The total patient load per remote monitor remained unclear, raising comparisons to surveillance dystopia.


The report examines Oxevision, a camera-based system that estimates pulse and breathing rates, as an example of remote monitoring technology. Now used in hundreds of US and UK inpatient facilities, the system has been connected to four deaths at UK mental health wards under investigation by the Lampard Inquiry. LIO, the company behind Oxevision, clarified that while patients died in rooms equipped with its technology, coroners attributed no deaths directly to the system itself. Some coroners noted staff may have relied on automated monitoring instead of required face-to-face checks.


- Timpani scheduling AI operational in 130+ HCA hospitals as of late 2026
- Study based on 76 total nurse participants across focus groups and workshops
- Four UK deaths in facilities using Oxevision monitoring under investigation
- FDA cleared Oxevision vital signs monitoring as moderate-risk medical device


## Accountability Gaps in Healthcare AI


The research highlights a troubling pattern: hospitals deploy AI tools rapidly without informing nurses of changes, independent evidence of effectiveness remains scarce, and responsibility when systems fail stays undefined. I. Glenn Cohen, a Harvard Law School professor specializing in health law and bioethics, noted that even well-validated tools may perform differently across settings due to variations in staffing, patient populations, and resources. He emphasized hospitals must test tools locally and maintain ongoing monitoring after deployment.


Wells stressed that participating nurses are not anti-technology. They "desperately love things that make their lives easier" and praised AI tools with clear patient benefits, such as continuous glucose monitors. The core issue centers on implementation without clinical input and systems that may shift blame to individual nurses when failures occur.


## What This Means


This report arrives as public skepticism toward AI hardens across sectors. Recent US midterm voters supported data center limits in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, while major school districts in New York City and Los Angeles imposed sweeping AI restrictions this fall. In healthcare, the findings suggest that AI pitched as a remedy for understaffing may instead degrade nursing work when deployed without transparency, accountability frameworks, or frontline worker input. The research underscores the need for hospitals to include doctors, nurses, and patients in AI adoption decisions before tools reshape the fundamental nature of healthcare professions.
